summary: This paper proposes suppressing idling errors in superconducting qubits through circuit scheduling that adjusts the timing of Hadamard gates within idle intervals, without inserting additional control pulses. Two strategies are introduced—midpoint placement and random shot-by-shot placement—and validated on a 64-qubit superconducting processor with measured coherence times $T_1 = 5.24$–$32.81$ μs and $T_2 = 8.44$–$43.34$ μs, showing improvements up to 12% in accuracy compared to unfavorable placements.
motivation: Idling errors from amplitude damping, dephasing, and frequency drift accumulate when qubits remain inactive during circuit execution, particularly in circuits requiring SWAP gates for quantum error correction. Dynamical decoupling mitigates this but introduces gate-fidelity errors; a control-free alternative is needed.
method: Two heuristic scheduling rules are proposed: placing H gates at the temporal midpoint of idle intervals, or sampling insertion times uniformly over each shot and averaging outcomes. The density-matrix evolution under combined amplitude damping ($\gamma = 1 - e^{-t/T_1}$), dephasing ($\lambda = 1 - e^{-t/T_2}/2$), and quasi-static detuning ($\delta\omega$) is analytically derived; trace distance is used to quantify fidelity loss. Hardware experiments on single- and two-qubit circuits, plus QuTiP simulations with Haar-random initial states, validate the approach.
result: Midpoint placement and random placement both yield near-optimal performance in the practically relevant regime ($T \lesssim 6$ μs for two-qubit states), avoiding worst-case exposure to either amplitude damping or dephasing. For unknown initial states, both strategies reduce Haar-averaged trace distance by up to 12% at $T = 5$ μs; analytical results confirm that the midpoint achieves the global minimum when accumulated phase $\omega T \leq \pi/2$ and remains robust beyond this via symmetry-breaking effects that typically shift the optimum by $< 1\%$.
